new_statements.quote: 我们用 SFS 对布兴语的次要音节做语音分析，证明王洪君先生对汉语前冠音节的韵律说明同样适合于布兴语的词要[sic]音节。即：布兴语的词要[sic]音节在音长上较短，（如果次要音节本身含有鼻音、边音韵尾，则音长会长一些，但跟主要音节的音长相比仍然是短音节。）在音强上，布兴语的次要音节一般比主要音节弱，而音高上次要音节跟主要音节的音高没有明显的区别，基本一致。
new_statements.translation: We used SFS to make a phonetic analysis of the Buxing minor syllable, which shows that Wang Hongjun's prosodic characterisation of Chinese 'front-crown' syllables applies equally to the Buxing minor syllable. That is: the Buxing minor syllable is shorter in duration (if the minor syllable itself has a nasal or lateral coda its duration is somewhat longer, but compared with the major syllable it is still a short syllable); in intensity the Buxing minor syllable is generally weaker than the major syllable; and in pitch there is no clear difference between the minor and the major syllable - they are basically the same. [Corroboration, Lao Bit: Badenoch 2016: 5-23, p. 6: "Bit is a disyllabic, iambic language, with many onset clusters and a rich system of morphology."]
new_statements.citation: 高永奇 Gao Yongqi. 2004. 布兴语的次要音节 [The minor syllable of Buxing]. 语言科学 Linguistic Sciences 3(4): 84-96. Anyang Normal University / journal of Jiangsu Normal University.
new_statements.locator: p. 85, section 2.2 布兴语次要音节的语音特点 (verified against the page image, PDF page 2)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (13 pp., image-only, journal pp. 84-96) opened; PDF page 2 = journal p. 85 rendered with page render at 150 dpi and read visually. Section 2.2 布兴语次要音节的语音特点 contains the quoted passage verbatim, from 我们用 SFS 对布兴语的次要音节做语音分析 through 音高上次要音节跟主要音节的音高没有明显的区别，基本一致。 The reader's transcription matches the page image exactly, including the original's typo 词要音节 (twice, for 次要音节) and 韵律说明 (the scanned file mis-reads this as 前律说明; the page reads 韵律). The same paragraph first cites Svantesson & Karlsson 2004 on Kammu minor:major duration ratios of about 1:4-1:5 with identical pitch, then gives the Buxing SFS result: minor syllable shorter (longer if it has a nasal/lateral coda, but still short relat…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Buxing/Bit words are mono- or sesquisyllabic (minor syllable + major syllable); the major, i.e. final, syllable carries the prominence, and the minor syllable is short, reduced and weaker in intensity, with no pitch distinction. Badenoch (2016: 6) sums the Lao variety up as 'disyllabic, iambic', and Sidwell 2015: 55 (second-hand via Wikipedia) states that stress falls on the final syllable. Gao does not use the term 重音 'stress'; his statement is a phonetic characterisation of the minor vs. major syllable rather than a stress rule for polysyllabic compounds.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Gao notes that minor syllables with a nasal or lateral coda are somewhat longer but still short relative to the major syllable; Gao also observes minor syllables being reduced, dropped or merged with the major syllable in word formation (pp. 84, 93-95).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: sesquisyllabic phonological word (minor + major syllable) in citation/elicited forms, with acoustic measurements on single words (e.g. tʃɿ liaŋ 'moon', p. 85). Badenoch's 'iambic' applies to the disyllabic word. No phrase-level statement. Tone: Gao's article makes no tone claim for Buxing; Wikipedia (from Sidwell 2015: 55-57) reports no tones or registers for either variety.
new_statements.identity_note: buxi1237 is a Glottolog 'Bookkeeping' entry for the retired ISO code bxt 'Buxinhua' (= Chinese 布兴语 Buxing), merged into Bit [bgk] by ISO 639-3 CR 2007-009 (adopted 2008-01-14); the language-level code of record is bitt1240 (Bit / Khabit, Austroasiatic > Palaungic > Bit-Khang), so any catalog entry should be filed under bitt1240 rather than this retired key. The deciding source (Gao 2004) describes the Mengla County, Yunnan variety (Buxing, 539 speakers in 2000); the corroborating source (Badenoch 2016) describes Lao Bit of Ban Bompiang, Luang Namtha, which Badenoch calls 'a closely related dialect' of the same language. The sister language Kháng [kjm] (khan1274) is a different language and is tonal.

sources.note: p. 85 sect. 2.2 (acoustic analysis with SFS): the minor syllable is short, generally weaker in intensity than the major (final) syllable, and has no clear pitch difference from it; p. 84 quotes Wang Jingliu that minor syllables are 'usually read light' (轻读). No explicit 重音 rule; no tone statement for Buxing.

Second-hand: "Stress falls on the final syllable. No tones or registers were reported." citing Sidwell 2015 p. 55 (a summary of Badenoch 2015); Buxing (Gao 2004) said to be the same language, both sesquisyllabic and atonal (citing Sidwell 2015 p. 57).
